cheatsheet:
**Stack vs heap**
Local variables vanish when their function returns. Heap memory stays until you `free` it.

**Asking for memory**
`int *a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));` · `calloc(n, sizeof(int))` also zeroes it · always check for `NULL`

**Growing**
`int *bigger = realloc(a, new_n * sizeof(int)); if (bigger == NULL) { ... } a = bigger;`

**Giving it back**
`free(a);` exactly once per block. Don't use `a` afterwards (dangling pointer).

**Linked list**
`typedef struct Node { int value; struct Node *next; } Node;` · walk with `for (Node *p = head; p != NULL; p = p->next)` · save `next` before freeing a node

lessons.title: Asking for memory: malloc and free
lessons.concept:
So far every variable lived on the **stack**: made when a function starts, wiped when it returns. That's why an array's size had to be known up front.

The **heap** is memory you ask for while the program runs: `int *cells = malloc(n * sizeof(int));` asks for room for n ints and gives you the address. If there's no memory left you get `NULL`, so always check.

Heap memory stays until **you** hand it back with `free(cells);`. Forget, and it leaks: that's this mission's reactor leak.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: The cells hold 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16, which add up to 30.

drills.prompt: On the judge an `int` is 4 bytes. How many bytes does this ask for?
drills.explain: `sizeof(int)` is 4, times 5 ints is 20 bytes. Letting `sizeof` do the maths means you never hard-code the 4.

drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so this asks for room for 3 doubles, then gives it back. It prints `22.5`.
drills.explain: `malloc` takes a number of bytes, `sizeof(double)` says how big one double is, and `free` gives the block back.

drills.prompt: `make_readings` builds the readings, but the program crashes as soon as main uses them. Read the compiler's warning, then fix it.
drills.explain: `readings` lived on make_readings' stack, which is wiped the moment it returns, so main got an address of nothing (gcc even warns: *function returns address of local variable*). Memory from `malloc` survives the return, and main frees it.

drills.prompt: Read `n`, then `n` numbers into memory from `malloc`. Print them back **in reverse order** on one line, separated by spaces, then free the memory.
drills.explain: Use the heap block exactly like an array: `values[i]`. The only fiddly part is the spaces: print one between numbers, not after the last.

lessons.title: Memory that grows: calloc and realloc
lessons.concept:
`calloc(n, sizeof(int))` is malloc that also sets every byte to **0**. Plain `malloc` gives you whatever junk was there.

When a block is full, `realloc(log, new_size)` makes it bigger. It may move your data to a new address, so use what it returns. Doubling the size each time keeps the moves rare.

Catch the result in a **new** pointer first: if realloc fails it returns `NULL`, and `log = realloc(log, ...)` would lose your only pointer to the old block.

predict.prompt: It's fed `4 8 15 16 23 42 0`. Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: Six readings arrive. Room grows 2 → 4 when the third arrives, then 4 → 8 for the fifth.

drills.explain: calloc zeroes the whole block, so the two untouched ints are 0.

drills.prompt: Why catch realloc's result in `bigger` instead of writing `log = realloc(log, size);`?
options: If realloc fails it returns NULL, and you'd lose your only pointer to the old block
realloc can only store into a brand-new variable
It makes realloc faster
`log` can't be changed after malloc
drills.answer: If realloc fails it returns NULL, and you'd lose your only pointer to the old block
drills.explain: On failure the old block is still there and still yours. Overwriting `log` with NULL leaks it.

drills.prompt: Fill the blanks to grow the block safely.
drills.explain: `realloc` returns the (maybe moved) bigger block, or `NULL` if there's no memory.

drills.prompt: Readings arrive until a `0` (you don't know how many). Store them, growing the block when it's full. Then print every reading **strictly above the average**, one per line, in the order they came. If there are none, print `none`.
drills.explain: You need every reading stored before you know the average, hence the growing block. `value * count > sum` compares with the average without any decimals.

lessons.title: Linked lists: nodes that point to nodes
lessons.concept:
A **linked list** is a chain of small heap blocks. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node; the last one points to `NULL`.

Adding at the front is cheap: make a node, point it at the old head, and it becomes the new head. Walking the list is `for (Node *p = head; p != NULL; p = p->next)`.

Freeing needs care: save `head->next` **before** `free(head)`, because after free you're not allowed to look inside that node.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: Each push goes in front, so the last one pushed (3) comes first.

drills.prompt: Order and indent the lines to free a whole list without touching freed memory.
drills.explain: Remember where the rest of the chain is, free this node, then move on.

options: It reads `head->next` from a node that's already been freed
Nothing, it frees the list
free needs the size of the node
It frees the next node instead
drills.answer: It reads `head->next` from a node that's already been freed
drills.explain: After `free(head)` the node isn't yours any more, so `head->next` is a **dangling pointer** read. Save next first.

drills.prompt: This should print how many nodes the list has and their sum. It's one short, and an empty list crashes it. Fix the loop.
drills.explain: `p->next != NULL` stops before the last node, and with an empty list `p` is NULL, so `p->next` crashes. Test `p != NULL`.

drills.prompt: Finish `largest`: return the biggest value in a list that has at least one node. `main` is done.
drills.explain: Start `best` at the first node's value (not 0, the readings might all be negative), then walk the rest.

checkpoint.prompt: Which rule keeps a program leak-free?
options: Every block from malloc, calloc or realloc gets exactly one free
Free every pointer variable at the end of main
Only free memory in long programs
Free each block twice to be safe
checkpoint.answer: Every block from malloc, calloc or realloc gets exactly one free
checkpoint.explain: One block, one free. Freeing twice is a bug too.
The block holds 0 3 6 9. `q` points at element 2 (6), and `q[1]` is the one after it (9).

options: A dangling pointer: it still holds the old address, but using it is a bug
Automatically set to NULL
A pointer to a fresh block
Gone, along with the variable
checkpoint.answer: A dangling pointer: it still holds the old address, but using it is a bug
checkpoint.explain: free gives the memory back but leaves `p` unchanged. Some people write `p = NULL;` straight after to be safe.
Pushing at the front reverses the order: the list is 7 → 6 → 5.

checkpoint.prompt: A function mallocs a block, stores the address in a local pointer, and returns without freeing it or handing it back. What's that called?
options: A memory leak
A dangling pointer
A stack overflow
A segmentation fault
checkpoint.explain: Nobody has the address any more, so the block can never be freed: it leaks a little every call.
